text: From the full text of the paper: [Isometric exercise training] programmes commonly employ protocols of 4×2min contractions, separated by 1–4min rest intervals, performed three times a week. [Isometric handgrip] is often prescribed at 30% maximum voluntary contraction, while [isometric wall squat] and [isometric leg extension] protocols are typically performed at 95% of the peak heart rate achieved during a laboratory-based maximal incremental isometric exercise test. The [isometric wall squat] may also be prescribed using a self-selected wall squat, with a knee joint angle that would elicit a rate of perceived exertion (RPE) of 3.5–4.5/10 for bout 1; RPE 5–6/10 for bout 2; RPE of 6.5–7.5/10 for bout 3 and RPE of 8–9/10 for bout 4. As for whether the effects are additive, they're likely only partially additive. For example, aerobic training was found to cause an average 4.49/2.53mm Hg reduction, dynamic resistance training was found to cause an average 4.55/3.04mm Hg reduction, but combined aerobic and resistance training only caused an average 6.04/2.54mm Hg reduction, rather than the 9.04/5.57mm Hg reduction that you'd expect if they were perfectly additive.

text: Both camps are describing the same program, which is why it looks contradictory. GZCLP is flexible on purpose here. The simple version: tier 1 is your heavy main lift for the day (the 10-15 total reps you mentioned), and tier 2 is the volume work for the same muscle groups, done lighter with more total reps (the 20-30). Tier 2 exists to build the muscle that drives the tier 1 lift. The standard template pairs complementary lifts on the same day — T1 squat with T2 bench, T1 overhead press with T2 deadlift, and so on — so you're spreading volume across the week instead of doing the same lift heavy and for volume in one session. That's the pairing you'll see in most writeups. For the tier 2 exercise itself, same lift or a close variation both count. Same lift means more direct practice on the movement; a variation like front squat, incline bench, or close-grip bench is a way to hammer a weak point. A lot of people run the same lift until something stalls, then swap in a variation. Neither choice is "wrong" per the program. The part that actually matters: tier 2 stays submaximal and progresses on its own — add reps first, then weight — independent of what's happening on tier 1. Don't turn it into a second heavy day and you'll be fine either way.
label: evidence

text: They train related qualities, but they are not interchangeable. An inverted row is mainly a horizontal pull; a pull-up is a vertical pull. If the goal is a first pull-up, some form of assisted vertical pulling should usually be the more specific exercise, while rows remain useful additional work for the upper back and elbow flexors. The machine is not automatically safer simply because it is assisted. The useful version is the one that lets you train a comfortable range of motion with a load you can control. If a particular machine forces your forearms into an uncomfortable position or repeatedly produces a hard elbow pop, I would not keep trying to make that machine fit you. A neutral-grip pulldown, foot-assisted pull-up from a box, or another setup that lets the hands and shoulder blades move naturally may suit you better. For a weak or injury-prone beginner, I would keep both movement patterns but scale them conservatively: a few clean sets of an assisted vertical pull, followed by inclined rows at an angle you can control. Finish each set before form changes, and progress only one thing at a time—slightly less assistance, one more repetition, or a slightly lower row angle. The main criterion is not which device looks most like a pull-up. It is whether you can repeat pain-free, controlled reps and gradually increase the amount of your own bodyweight you handle.
label: claim

text: Shorter rests shift the circuit more toward the cardio end of things. That's basically the whole mechanism. When you rest 60-90 seconds between stations, your heart rate comes back down a good chunk each time. Cut that to 30-45 seconds and your heart rate stays elevated for the whole circuit — which is what trains cardiovascular endurance. The 30-60 second range is the sweet spot most people land on for that conditioning effect. A couple practical notes: Go too short (like 10-15 seconds) and your form falls apart before your heart gets the benefit. Sloppy reps on a circuit aren't worth it. This works best with moderate weights. Circuit training is for conditioning, not max strength — if you need full rest to keep your numbers up, that's a strength session, not a circuit. A decent gauge: you should be breathing hard but able to talk in short phrases during the work. If you're completely gassed and can't get words out, add a little rest. If you could hold a normal conversation, cut some rest.

text: There are several formulae out there for "max heart rate" and truth be told, they all are nothing but an approximation. If you want a better approximation, this paper gives a solid analysis of research data coupled with a laboratory study, delivering 208-(0.7x[age]) as the best linear approximation, which gives 170 for your age. Neither gender nor training status played any role. The individual case can be different, this is just natural individual variation. Natural measures taken over a big enough population tend to be distributed in a Bell curve (normal distribution). As you can see in the plot in the linked paper, page 154, there are maxHRs at peak physical exertion around and above 180 for ages between 50 and 55. When I train at my lactate threshold (max intensity, interval training etc.), I do commonly go beyond the 181 suggested for my age by this formula. For minutes. Generally, general truths apply to the general population. Every individual is different (within limits). That being said, important measures are the time for return to baseline HR after the activity and maxHR reached during the activity. You can use a simple fitness tracker band for approximate values to check these. A chest band for more precise values would be a choice if you are really worried about your heart rates. Suppose your heart rate does not significantly (>12 BPM) decrease within the first minute(s) after you stop any activity. In that case, this may be more of a reason to worry since that is, in fact, linked to mortality.

text: Biomechanically, as far as the ground reaction force the muscles have to deal with, it obviously does not make a difference. That said, four points to consider: Even if you had mainly trained the upper body, the lower extremities always get stronger with weight. Normally, the quads can generate 2.5-3 kn/kg body weight. That's just because they are used a lot in daily life. If you had had the gains solely in the lower body, there may have been potential to optimise muscle economy while running, the effects of which may have compensated for the other factors a bit. Of course, more muscle tissue allows for more power, yet it also consumes more energy than fat, even if at rest Since your steady state energy generation capacity is capped on a systemic level (think VO2max), and you have a higher energy consumption due to higher ground reaction forces (main contributor) and base energy consumption (minor influence). Anything that is used there cannot go into performance. There are other factors at play, like additional vascular volume (higher in fat tissue), higher peak ground reaction forces due to "wobbling" of fat, higher inflammation factors due to fat tissue, higher peak forces in joints, less favourable force levers due to sheer body circumference, etc. - yet they are negligible when talking about the ratios and relative gains taken into consideration here. Thus, generally, we can and should say that fat is worse than muscle for running. It just does not make much of a difference in your case.

text: Nah, they're two different things. Soreness is mostly just your body reacting to something new, especially the lowering part of lifts. It usually peaks a day or two after and then fades, and after a few weeks of the same workouts you barely get sore at all anymore. That's the repeated bout effect. The muscle is still growing. It just stops complaining. Actual recovery, your muscles being ready to produce force again, usually happens way before the soreness goes away. For normal gym work it's typically within a day or two. So here's the practical test. If you can hit your planned weights and your form feels solid, you're good to train even if you're still a little sore. Chasing zero soreness before every session will just have you waiting around for no reason. And the flip side is true too. No soreness doesn't automatically mean you're recovered. You can run yourself into the ground with zero soreness, especially on frequent heavy training. The thing to actually watch is your performance. If your numbers keep dropping session to session, that's the real signal to back off or take a rest day. Short version: don't schedule your workouts by soreness. Schedule them by how the bar moves.
label: evidence

text: Short answer: they're good enough for picking training weights, but they're not a real tested 1RM. Most calculators use Epley or Brzycki-style formulas. They work best when the set is in the 3–8 rep range. Once you get up around 10–12+ reps, the estimate starts getting loose. Squats and deadlifts usually get under-predicted a bit, smaller lifts like overhead press can get over-predicted, and it depends a lot on the lifter. Also, if the set was sloppy, done after other work, or taken to ugly failure, the number gets less trustworthy. Two people can have the same 5RM and still have a true 1RM that's off by like 5–15%. I'd use a calculator to set working percentages, then adjust by how the sets feel. If you need an exact max for a meet or a real test day, work up to a heavy single, or hit a clean 2–3RM and convert from there.

text: Do you actually need to train the same muscles in different planes of motion? Well, no, but you don't "need" to workout at all. What are your goals ("strength" and "hypertrophy" are not the most specific things)? FWIW, most hypertrophy-oriented people I know do five separate delt exercises and three or four calf exercises where the differences are things like "toes in vs out", "standing vs sitting", etc. Different planes of motion (usually) work different parts of the muscle and/or work different abutting muscles. OHP, bench, and bar dips are basically the same motion in 90 degree increments; would your goals be met if you just did bench? Why would I, in my example, get an injury from a horizontal pull if I primarily do vertical pulling? I'd say it's not so much "get an injury" as "fail to avoid a potential injury". A pull up primarily hits the teres major, lats, and biceps. A barbell row primarily hits the traps, rear delts, and rhomboids (and some of the lower erector spinae, depending on how heavy you go). Though there's some "halo" effect on all of these. If you do something that might hurt your traps, but you think it will be fine because you do lots of pull ups, you may get hurt. There is some risk of overuse injuries, but that's mostly handled by antagonistic exercises (e.g. OHP & pull ups).

text: this sounds very similar to proximal hamstring tendinopathy ("yoga butt"), which is pretty common when people push deep forward folds too quickly. Your nervous system does help regulate flexibility, but if you repeatedly push past your tissue's current capacity, the tendon where the hamstring attaches to the sit bone can become overloaded. That's why the pain is usually at the attachment point, not throughout the muscle. Nerves can become irritated too, but they're rarely the primary structure injured in this type of overuse problem. The frustrating part is that tendons heal more slowly than muscles because they have a relatively limited blood supply. Complete rest usually isn't the answer, though. Most sports medicine specialists recommend temporarily avoiding deep stretches, then gradually rebuilding tendon strength with a physical therapist or a progressive loading program. If the pain has been lingering for weeks or is getting worse, it's worth seeing a sports medicine physician or physio. Helpful resources: Mayo Clinic – Hamstring Injury Overview Physiopedia – Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy NHS – Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy

text: The study “Do the anatomical and physiological properties of a muscle determine its adaptive response to different loading protocols?” examined this exact topic. In the study, young untrained men trained calves in 4 sets of 6–10 or 20–30 repetitions. There was no difference in calf muscle thickness between the groups. This study is one of 23 studies that explored the effects of different loads (and therefore rep ranges) on site-specific muscular hypertrophy that were examined in the influential review paper “Loading Recommendations for Muscle Strength, Hypertrophy, and Local Endurance: A Re-Examination of the Repetition Continuum”. This paper concluded that there is no ideal number of repetitions for hypertrophy in general. To quote directly from the “Conclusions” section, With respect to hypertrophy, the compelling body of literature indicates that similar whole muscle growth (i.e., muscle thickness, CSA) can be achieved across a wide spectrum of loading ranges. The researchers recommend moderate loads (and number of repetitions) from a practical standpoint.

text: Two years of steady 5/3/1 and the stall shows up right when the cut starts? That's not a programming problem, that's a calorie problem. Nobody adds weight to the bar while losing weight. If your lifts are just holding still while you're down 3 kg, the program is actually doing its job. So first: stop grading the program on cut performance. You won't know whether 5/3/1 has run its course until you've been back at maintenance for a few weeks. That said, if the goal is genuinely hypertrophy now, Triumvirate is an odd pick anyway. It's a low-volume template - main sets, one assistance lift, go home. 5/3/1 works fine for size, but you want the volume flavors: the 5x10 assistance work at lower percentages, or just more assistance volume in general. Three heavy sets a day was never a mass program. One thing worth checking regardless of which template you run: your training max. The rule is 90% of your true 1RM, and most people creep it up too high over a couple of years. Then every week is a grinder and progress dies. Knocking your TM back 5-10% and rebuilding is the oldest fix in the book. Week 1's top set is 85% of your TM, which is only about 76% of your true max - that's supposed to move fast, not feel like a test. Practical take: keep 5/3/1 through the cut, judge it after. If hypertrophy is really the goal, either swap to a higher-volume template or park 5/3/1 for a few months and run something built around volume. Just pick one goal at a time - you can't chase size and a deficit simultaneously.

text: All things being equal (depth in the water, not breaking the surface with the kick, travelling in a straight line, symmetry of the kick), both standard and side dolphin will be the same speed. However, many swimmers do not execute the two identically: standard dolphin may have kicks that break the surface, reducing efficiency swimmers may have a stronger posterior or anterior kick, which affects standard dolphin differently than side dolphin side dolphin may be difficult for a swimmer to maintain in a straight line, either requiring slower more concentrated swimming to stay straight, or traversing a longer path And all of this changes if you need to include breaths. Only you can know which one you're faster at. Since you've asked on fitness.SE, I assume you are interested in improving your performance, not simply which movement is faster. It is dubious that you would choose an exercise to improve performance based on which is faster, or which is more efficient. In fact, often, one intentionally chooses a less efficient variant to experience extra or non-standard loading. You should choose an exercise or variant based on what change you're trying to create in your performance. See the programming tag for questions about exercise selection. Regardless, efficiency and speed do not go hand-in-hand. For example, sprinting is faster than jogging, but jogging is more efficient. Which you should choose depends on what you're trying to improve.

text: The rule you're talking about is the IPF's 2023 change: at the bottom of the rep, the elbows have to drop below the top of the shoulder joint. It was aimed squarely at the extreme-arch, ultra-wide-grip benches where the bar barely moved. And like the comment says, judging it is genuinely fuzzy — it's a visual call from the side of the platform, and when it first came in even experienced judges weren't calling it consistently. Since you can't control the judging, control your margin: Set up for your stiff days, not your best days. If thoracic mobility swings a bit with your warmup, pick an arch height and grip width where you're clearly under the line even when you're tight. A setup that only passes on a perfect warmup is a gamble at a meet. Wider grip and bigger arch shrink your margin. A narrower grip gives the elbows more vertical travel, which makes it easier to clearly sink below the shoulder line. Film yourself from the side at bench height. That's roughly the same angle the judge gets. Check where the elbows sit relative to the top of the shoulder joint at the bottom of the pause. Warm up the same way every time. A consistent routine means less day-to-day mobility swing, so your setup lands in the same place on meet day. One caveat: not every fed adopted this one. If you compete outside the IPF, read your own federation's rulebook for the division you're in — bench rules on arch, grip, and commands vary more than people expect.

text: Since you mention that you are doing high-intensity training where you take each set to failure, what you describe is completely normal. Make sure that you get adequate rest between sets. Generally, you want to rest between 30 seconds and 5 minutes between each set. Since you are doing a difficult workout, you want to be in the upper range, especially with compound exercises like weighted pullups. The study “Rest interval between sets in strength training” advocates for 3–5 minutes for maximum muscular power. If you are resting less than that, you will not be able to do the same amount of repetitions to failure as the previous set. Also, ensure your muscles are not fatigued before starting your workout. Allow at least 24–48 hours for a muscle group to recover before training it again. Additionally, make sure you get enough sleep.

If you're actually gonna test — like for a meet or just to see where you're at — do it right. Rack with the safeties set just below your range of motion, warm up with smaller and smaller sets as the weight climbs (don't gas yourself on the way up), and take small jumps near the top. 5–10 lbs on upper body stuff, 10–20 on squats and deads. First real miss, you're done. Trying to grind through a second miss just beats you up. Beginners especially: just estimate. Your max changes every few weeks anyway when you're new, so a big test day tells you a number that's already out of date.

text: Both, honestly. There's local fatigue and general/systemic fatigue, and they stack on each other. Local fatigue is the simple one: the muscles you just hammered are cooked for a bit. That's why bench right after heavy 5x5 squats tanks even though your chest is fresh. The general kind is the sneaky one. Heavy compounds beat up your whole system, not just the muscles, and that takes longer than a day to clear. Bench suffering the day after heavy squats isn't just a leg drive thing, your body is still carrying the tab from yesterday. Practical way I think about it: Soreness that never quite clears, joints getting cranky, sleep getting worse instead of better, and dreading sessions you normally like. Any one of those alone is nothing. A few of them together, for a week-plus, means fatigue is running ahead of recovery. When that happens, a deload week earns its keep: same movements, roughly half the sets, keep the weights honest but leave 3-4 reps in the tank on everything, skip the grinding. Technique week, basically. And don't stack your two heaviest compound days back to back if you can help it. Put the stuff you care about most first in the session. What it's not is a week on the couch eating like trash and sleeping five hours a night. That just digs the hole deeper.

text: I suffered from shin splints and a stress fracture when I got back to running after 15 years of less than healthy habits. My physical therapist noted that I had bad running form that was contributing to my injuries. He recommended multiple things, including increasing running cadence to improve my running form. But for me, the secret to good form wasn't running cadence. Instead, the reverse was true. When I finally figured out how to run correctly, my average cadence went from 160 to 175 over the next year. I am generally between 175 and 180 now. I have been running for many years now, and was even able to qualify for Boston. What may be obvious to many, but took me painful experience to learn is: Running with good form allows for consistent exercise without injury Running injury free consistently results in faster times and better metrics It's harder to improve running by changing metrics than it is to improve metrics by running correctly and consistently So don't focus too much on metrics when you are starting out. The data is good and the best running efficiency may actually be in the 170-180 range. But that data includes really good recreational runners and elite athletes who are on a different level than where you are now. For someone who has 'just gotten back into running', focusing on consistency and avoiding injury are far more important. Everything else will fall into place in time.

text: Jumping rope and doing the same movements without a rope may look similar, but they are not quite the same exercise. The rope provides an external rhythm and timing cue, forcing you to coordinate your jumps with your hands and feet. It also gives immediate feedback: if your timing is wrong, you hit the rope. Without a rope, you can still train the basic bouncing motion, coordination, and calf endurance, but there is less emphasis on timing and hand-foot coordination. Jumping rope also tends to encourage a consistent, light rhythm and can make the exercise more engaging. For sports such as boxing or Muay Thai, the rope is useful not only for cardio but also for developing rhythm, footwork, coordination, and the ability to stay relaxed while moving.

text: The stretch in your calves during the good morning exercise comes from the tension placed on the calf muscles, particularly the gastrocnemius, as they work to stabilize the ankle joint. In the good morning exercise, you’re hinging at the hips with a mostly straight leg, which lengthens the hamstrings and also affects the posterior chain of muscles, including the calves. The gastrocnemius muscle crosses both the knee and the ankle joints, so even though the knee doesn’t change position significantly, any movement that stretches the posterior chain (like hip flexion) can increase tension through this entire pathway. When you lean forward, the angle of your ankle joint changes slightly, especially if you shift your weight back onto your heels for balance, which increases the dorsiflexion (upward flex) angle at the ankle. This subtle change can further stretch the calf muscles, which is likely what you’re feeling during the movement.

text: I am a College T&F/XC Coach, and a runner myself for 16+ years. A classic workout that many milers like yourself will end up doing in their career is a classic workout that the famous Roger Bannister (1st sub-4:00 miler) would run, and it is perfectly scalable for all milers at all levels of fitness. Here's the workout. 10x400m on a 3-minute clock. That's it. Regardless of splits, you start a 400m interval at the top of every 3 minutes for 10 repeats. If you go faster, you get more rest, and slower, then you get less rest. This is what we call an Indicator Workout, meaning that whatever you can average for this workout per 400m is what you should be able to run 4 times in a row with zero rest. Here's the goal you should shoot for if you want to break 5:00 in the mile. 10x400m @1:15 per 400m on a 3-minute clock. If you accomplish this workout at the specified time, then you'll know you've got the fitness to run the time you want. Roger Bannister did this workout and averaged around 59 seconds before he ran sub-4. This has accurately predicted both my own mile times and the mile times of the athletes I've coached, almost to the millisecond. As you get faster, you can return to this workout and shoot for something quicker, like 1:10 (4:40 mile pace) and 1:05 (4:20 pace).

text: Switch to an auto regulation program. The premise of linear progression programs like Starting Strength and SL 5x5 is actually kind of silly when you think about it for a minute. They have you increasing intensity while holding volume constant with complete disregard for your personal rate of adaptation. And so for everyone, they eventually result in an intensity that is inappropriate for your level of fitness. Instead, switch to an auto regulated approach to load selection. The most common method used here is the RPE/RIR (rate of perceived exertion/reps in reserve) method. The idea here is to choose your working weight such that most of your sets are in the 6-9 RPE (1-4 RIR) range. With practice, you get better at finding the right weight, and most importantly, this method of load selection takes into account your overall level of fitness and day-to-day changes in your strength. As you get stronger (that is, adapt), you will naturally add weight to the bar, but in response to adaptation, rather than trying to “force” adaptation but arbitrarily increasing weight because the plan said you have to lift more than last time. For more details and some sample training, Barbell Medicine’s Beginner Prescription has some great info and a basic template for setting up a beginner training program. See the section on load selection and RPE for more detailed guidance on using the method than what I’ve provided here. (Disclosure: I am not associated with BBM. They just have great information).

text: Pull-ups and lat pull-downs differ significantly in mechanics and muscle recruitment patterns. In pull-ups, the entire body is engaged as a single unit. Your core, shoulders, back muscles, and even legs work together to stabilize the movement. This additional engagement increases overall muscle recruitment. Studies also show that Closed Kinetic Chain exercises like the pull-up (where one extremity of the body is fixed while the rest of the body moves) lead to higher motor unit recruitment compared to Open Kinetic Chain movements (such as lat pull-downs), resulting in more efficient muscle contraction. In some machines the pulley ratio could also introduce mechanical friction. It seems on the machines with 1:1 ratio (only 1 pulley, so the weight on the stack is close to "true" weight) friction is almost negligible but it can be more noticeable on machines with more pulleys.

text: If you minimize saturated fat intake, you’ve already solved the problem. It’s pretty well documented that replacing saturated fats in the diet with unsaturated sources is a reliable way to reduce LDL and mitigate cardiovascular event risk. See the AHA Presidential Advisory on Dietary Fats and CVD: Multiple randomized clinical trials, meta-analyses, prospective observational studies, and animal studies all support the concept of replacement of dietary saturated fats with unsaturated fats to reduce cardiovascular disease. Reducing dietary saturated fat and replacing it with polyunsaturated vegetable oil reduced cardiovascular disease by around 30%, similar to results from statin therapy. Prospective observational studies showed that reducing saturated fat and replacing it with polyunsaturated or monounsaturated fat caused 25% and 15% reductions in coronary heart disease (CHD), respectively. Mortality overall and from other causes was also reduced. Exercise is good and has lots of cardiovascular and other general health benefits. But if you’ve already minimized your saturated fat intake and replaced it with unsaturated sources, you’ve already solved the cholesterol problem and I would expect further improvements in LDL from exercise to be pretty modest. But still, you should exercise anyway, as there are numerous other health benefits and non-lipid risk factors that exercise can impact.
label: evidence
